concepts.label: Secondary hyperalgesia is increased pain sensitivity in normal (uninjured) skin surrounding an area of tissue damage
concepts.definition: Secondary hyperalgesia is an exaggerated pain response to a stimulus applied to normal, uninjured skin surrounding (but not within) an area of tissue damage. Unlike primary hyperalgesia, which results from direct peripheral sensitisation of nociceptors within the damaged tissue itself, secondary hyperalgesia arises from central sensitisation — increased excitability of dorsal horn neurons receiving convergent input from the surrounding, undamaged skin — so the surrounding skin becomes painfully sensitive even though its own nociceptors were never directly injured.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute increased pain sensitivity in the normal skin surrounding an injury (not the injury itself) to secondary hyperalgesia, driven by central sensitisation.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing secondary hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain in the normal skin surrounding an injury, from central sensitisation) with primary hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain within the injured tissue itself, from peripheral nociceptor sensitisation) — the two share a mechanism family but occur in different tissue and by a different route.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q49, embedded-answer format ("N- <answer>\n<description>"), read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q49 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b), answer/topic stated before the stem, no printed distractors — this batch authors its own. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: Primary hyperalgesia results from sensitisation of peripheral nociceptors by inflammatory tissue products released at the site of injury
concepts.definition: Primary hyperalgesia is heightened pain sensitivity localised to the actual site of tissue injury (for example, a sunburn), produced by chemical mediators — prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and other inflammatory tissue products released by damaged cells — that lower the activation threshold of peripheral nociceptors at that site. Because the nociceptors themselves are sensitised, previously innocuous or mildly painful stimuli (such as the light pressure of clothing) are then perceived as markedly more painful.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute primary hyperalgesia at an injury site to peripheral nociceptor sensitisation by locally released inflammatory tissue products.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing primary hyperalgesia (peripheral nociceptor sensitisation, at the injury site) with secondary hyperalgesia (central sensitisation, in the surrounding normal skin) — the sunburn-and-jacket vignette this batch draws on tests the primary, peripheral mechanism specifically.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q50 (case vignette: sunburn, pain on wearing a jacket), embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q50 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b) as a sunburn/jacket case vignette, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement on the same (ipsilateral) side of the body as the lesion, unlike the cerebral cortex
concepts.definition: Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates voluntary movement of the limbs on its own (ipsilateral) side of the body, because cerebellar efferent pathways cross twice — once leaving the deep cerebellar nuclei toward the contralateral red nucleus/thalamus, and again when the corticospinal tract they influence subsequently decussates in the medulla — restoring a net ipsilateral relationship between hemisphere and limb. This is the opposite laterality to the cerebral motor cortex, which controls the contralateral side after a single decussation, and it is why a unilateral cerebellar lesion produces incoordination (ataxia, dysmetria) on the same side as the lesion.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the cerebellum coordinates ipsilateral limb movement (net double decussation), in contrast to the cerebral cortex's single-decussation contralateral control.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the cerebellum follows the same contralateral rule as the cerebral cortex — a cerebellar hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral, not contralateral, limb incoordination, the reverse of a cortical motor lesion.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q51, embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q51 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b), answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: A lesion of the primary motor cortex, such as an infarction of the cerebral cortex supplying it, causes contralateral spastic hemiplegia
concepts.article_title: Motor cortex lesion and contralateral hemiplegia
concepts.definition: The primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4) gives rise to corticospinal fibres that decussate at the medullary pyramids; a lesion of the cortex itself — for example, ischaemic infarction in the territory of the blood vessels supplying that part of the cortex — therefore produces an upper motor neuron syndrome of spastic paralysis (hemiplegia), exaggerated tendon reflexes, and an extensor plantar response on the contralateral side of the body. This is the same general upper motor neuron laterality rule that applies to a lesion anywhere along the corticospinal pathway above its medullary decussation, whether at the cortex itself or, as classically taught for the internal capsule, further downstream.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute contralateral spastic hemiplegia to a lesion (e.g. vascular infarction) of the primary motor cortex, the same upper motor neuron laterality rule as an internal capsule lesion.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing a primary motor CORTEX lesion (this concept) with an INTERNAL CAPSULE lesion — both are upper motor neuron lesions producing contralateral spastic hemiplegia by the same decussation rule, but they are different anatomic sites with different classic vascular territories (cortical branches of the MCA/ACA vs. lenticulostriate perforators), so they are kept as separate, related facts rather than merged.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q52, embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf. Cross-paper duplicate of the same-cluster EOM CNS FINAL PAPER 1 2024 item 7 ("Primary motor area- CL hemiplagia"), held rather than re-authored — see coverage/ASU-CNS-3-LEDGER.md.
concepts.evidence_gaps: Independent neurophysiology reference not yet attached. A related but anatomically distinct fact (internal capsule lesion → contralateral spastic hemiplegia) exists as a pending Alexandria AU-MED-203 concept (CON-NEU-152993798822B6, see field_notes) — reviewed and kept separate rather than merged, since the lesion site differs.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q52 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b) ("spastic paralysis - Infarction in blood vessels supplying the cerebral cortex") and, cross-paper, as item 7 of the same cluster's EOM - CNS FINAL PAPER 1 2024.pdf ("Primary motor area- CL hemiplagia") — the FINAL PAPER item is held as a duplicate of this concept, not re-authored. A related but anatomically distinct concept, internal capsule lesion causing contralateral spastic hemiplegia, exists pending in docs/Alexandria-Source-Imports/concept/AU-MED-203-anatomy-concepts.md (label "A lesion of the internal capsule causes spastic paralysis of the contralateral side of the body") — reviewed and kept as a separate concept (different lesion site, different classic vascular territory), not merged; noted for a future editorial pass, not treated as a duplicate here.

concepts.label: A unilateral lesion of the fasciculus gracilis causes ipsilateral, not contralateral, loss of vibration sense below the lesion
concepts.definition: Because dorsal column fibres (fasciculus gracilis for the lower limb, fasciculus cuneatus for the upper limb) ascend on the same side of the spinal cord and do not decussate until they form internal arcuate fibres in the lower medulla, a unilateral lesion of the fasciculus gracilis — for example, from cord compression or a demyelinating plaque — causes loss of vibration and proprioceptive sense on the ipsilateral (same) side of the body, below the level of the lesion, not the contralateral side. A right fasciculus gracilis lesion, for instance, produces loss of vibration sense in the right leg (including the right tibia), the mirror image of the crossed pattern seen with spinothalamic (pain/temperature) tract lesions.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that a unilateral dorsal column (fasciculus gracilis) lesion causes ipsilateral, not contralateral, loss of vibration sense below the lesion.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming a spinal cord sensory lesion always produces contralateral loss, as it does for the spinothalamic tract — the dorsal columns are uncrossed until the medulla, so their lesions produce ipsilateral loss, the opposite pattern (this is also the basis of the ipsilateral half of Brown-Séquard syndrome).
concepts.original_wording: Source Q54 ("vibration right tibia - sensation loss d.t Right gracile injury"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q54 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b), answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors. Related to but distinct from this lane's own cluster 1 anatomy concept CON-NEU-1DAEC8F42F6C4E (general gracile/cuneate pathway anatomy) — this concept tests the clinical laterality point (ipsilateral loss) specifically, not held as a duplicate. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: The afferent limb of the flexor withdrawal reflex is carried by free nerve endings (nociceptors)
concepts.definition: The flexor withdrawal reflex is a polysynaptic spinal reflex triggered by a noxious (painful) stimulus, such as touching a hot surface; its afferent (sensory) limb is carried by free nerve endings — the nociceptors that transduce noxious mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli — rather than by an encapsulated receptor. These afferents synapse on spinal interneurons that, in turn, excite flexor motor neurons of the stimulated limb (producing withdrawal) while reciprocally inhibiting its extensors, and cross the cord to drive the crossed extensor reflex in the opposite limb.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify free nerve endings (nociceptors) as the afferent receptor type for the flexor withdrawal reflex.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Muscle and reflex physiology
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the withdrawal reflex's nociceptive (free nerve ending) afferent limb with the stretch reflex's proprioceptive (muscle spindle) afferent limb — the two spinal reflexes are driven by different receptor types and have different circuit complexity (monosynaptic stretch reflex vs. polysynaptic withdrawal reflex).
concepts.original_wording: Source Q55 ("withdrawal free nerve - Reflex and afferent match together"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q55 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b), answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: Superficial reflexes such as the abdominal reflex are lost in an upper motor neuron lesion because they depend on an intact corticospinal tract
concepts.article_title: Superficial reflex loss in UMN lesions
concepts.definition: Superficial (cutaneous) reflexes, such as the abdominal reflex (contraction of the underlying abdominal muscles on stroking the overlying skin) and the cremasteric reflex, differ from deep tendon reflexes in that their reflex arc requires a functioning corticospinal tract input to the spinal segment, not just an intact peripheral nerve and spinal cord segment. Consequently, an upper motor neuron lesion that interrupts the corticospinal tract abolishes these superficial reflexes below the lesion, even as it simultaneously exaggerates the deep tendon reflexes (which do not share this corticospinal dependency) — loss of superficial reflexes together with hyperactive deep reflexes is a classic combined sign of an upper motor neuron lesion.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute the loss of superficial (e.g. abdominal) reflexes in an upper motor neuron lesion to their dependency on an intact corticospinal tract, contrasting with the simultaneous exaggeration of deep tendon reflexes.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming all reflexes behave the same way in an upper motor neuron lesion — deep tendon reflexes become exaggerated (loss of descending inhibition) while superficial reflexes are lost (loss of the corticospinal drive they specifically require); the two move in opposite directions in the same lesion.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q56, embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q56 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b) ("cause of loss of Superficial reflexes (like abdominal) in case of UMNL - intact corticospinal tract"), answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: Bradykinin (a kinin) is classically identified as a directly algesic (pain-producing) chemical mediator
concepts.definition: Bradykinin, a kinin generated from plasma kininogen at sites of tissue injury and inflammation, is one of the most potent directly algesic (pain-producing) chemical mediators: it acts on peripheral nociceptor terminals (via B2 receptors) to trigger pain signalling outright, not merely to lower their threshold to other stimuli. It also contributes to the peripheral sensitisation of nociceptors that underlies primary hyperalgesia, so its actions extend beyond direct pain production to amplifying pain from other stimuli.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify bradykinin (a kinin) as a directly algesic (pain-producing) chemical mediator released at sites of tissue injury.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing bradykinin's direct algesic action (triggering pain outright) with prostaglandin E2's sensitising action (lowering the nociceptor's threshold to other stimuli, without itself directly triggering pain) — both are inflammatory pain mediators, but by different mechanisms.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q57 ("Pain stimulating substance - Kinin"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.evidence_gaps: Independent neurophysiology reference not yet attached. A closely related pending Helwan HU-BMS-102 pathology concept (CON-INF-8E61F598EFD892, "Bradykinin is a principal mediator of inflammatory pain") exists but has no supporting article record anywhere in docs/Helwan-Source-Imports/article/ — every mint in this lane needs a teachable article, so this concept is minted fresh (own article) rather than reused via overlay, with the Helwan id logged as a rejected merge candidate for a future editorial pass once that lane's article gap is fixed.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q57 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b), answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors. A pending Helwan HU-BMS-102 pathology concept states the identical fact (CON-INF-8E61F598EFD892) but has no article of its own to link a question to, so this batch mints its own concept+article instead of reusing that one; the Helwan id is recorded as a rejected merge candidate, not silently ignored. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: The Pacinian corpuscle is the receptor chiefly responsible for detecting vibration
concepts.definition: The Pacinian corpuscle is a large, encapsulated, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor found in the deep dermis, subcutaneous tissue, and around joints and viscera; its onion-like lamellated capsule filters out sustained pressure and makes it selectively sensitive to high-frequency mechanical oscillation, so it is the receptor chiefly responsible for detecting vibration. This distinguishes it from other cutaneous mechanoreceptors — Meissner's corpuscles (light touch, lower-frequency flutter), Merkel discs (sustained pressure/texture), and Ruffini endings (skin stretch) — each tuned to a different mechanical modality.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify the Pacinian corpuscle as the mechanoreceptor chiefly responsible for detecting vibration.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the Pacinian corpuscle (vibration, rapidly adapting) with the muscle spindle (muscle length/stretch) or the Golgi tendon organ (muscle tension) — all three are mechanoreceptors, but each is tuned to a different specific stimulus.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q58, embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q58 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b) ("Receptor of vibration - Pacinian"), answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.

concepts.label: Golgi tendon organ (Ib) afferents inhibit the alpha motor neurons of the same muscle via a spinal inhibitory interneuron (autogenic inhibition)
concepts.definition: The Golgi tendon organ, situated in series with extrafusal muscle fibres at the musculotendinous junction, signals muscle tension via its Ib afferent fibres. These Ib afferents enter the spinal cord and synapse on an inhibitory interneuron, which in turn inhibits the alpha motor neurons supplying the same (homonymous) muscle — a disynaptic circuit, not a direct Ib-to-alpha-motor-neuron synapse — so that excessive tension in a muscle reflexively reduces its own contraction, a protective reflex termed autogenic (inverse myotatic) inhibition.
concepts.explicit_objective: Trace the Golgi tendon organ reflex arc: Ib afferent to an inhibitory interneuron to inhibition of the alpha motor neurons of the same muscle (autogenic inhibition), noting the circuit is disynaptic, not monosynaptic.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Muscle and reflex physiology
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the Golgi tendon organ's Ib afferents synapse directly on the alpha motor neuron, as the monosynaptic stretch reflex does — the tendon organ reflex is disynaptic, routed through an inhibitory interneuron, and it inhibits (not excites) the alpha motor neurons of the same muscle.
concepts.original_wording: Source Q61, embedded-answer format, read from EOM MCQs - PHYSIOLOGY CNS PAPER 1 MCQ.pdf.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Q61 of the ASU-CNS-3 Physiology CNS EOM MCQ compilation (src_db7dce81f0f09a0a630b) ("Inputs of Golgi tendon organ synapses with - Alpha motor neurons"), answer/topic stated before the stem. The printed key names the ultimate target (alpha motor neurons) without stating the intervening inhibitory interneuron; this batch's explanation supplies the standard disynaptic circuit rather than implying a direct synapse, flagged here as an author_notes doubt rather than silently corrected. Part of items 49-65, outside cluster 2's scoped first 48.
